title: How Close Can You Look?

patient.name: Miss Rachel Tan Hui Min
patient.presenting_complaint: New patient — eye strain, headaches, and intermittent double vision while reading and studying

history.hpc: Rachel reports that over the past semester, she has experienced increasing eye strain, frontal headaches, and occasional double vision when reading or using her laptop for prolonged periods (more than 30 minutes). The double vision resolves when she looks up and rests her eyes. She finds herself losing her place while reading and sometimes closing one eye to relieve the discomfort. Her distance vision is unaffected. She has been referred for a Near Point of Convergence (NPC) assessment as part of her orthoptic work-up.
history.pmhx: No previous eye surgery. No known ocular disease. Last eye check 2 years ago was normal. Wears glasses for mild myopia, mainly for distance.
history.social_hx: University student, studies 6-8 hours daily including screen time. Non-smoker.

iop.right: Not tested — not indicated for this visit
iop.left: Not tested — not indicated for this visit

npc_assessment.method: An accommodative target (small print or penlight with target) brought slowly towards the patient's eyes along the midline while she maintains fixation on it; the point at which one eye breaks fixation and drifts outward (or the patient reports diplopia) is recorded as the break point, and the point at which fusion is recovered as the target is moved away is the recovery point
npc_assessment.break_point: 16 cm from the bridge of the nose (3 trials, range 14-18 cm)
npc_assessment.normal_reference: Normal NPC break point is less than 10 cm
npc_assessment.result: NPC break point is significantly receded compared to normal (16 cm vs <10 cm expected), with poor recovery — consistent with convergence insufficiency

investigations.accommodation_note: Patient reports symptoms reproduced during testing (eye strain and momentary double vision at near)

diagnosis: Near Point of Convergence assessment completed over 3 trials, showing a consistently receded break point (16 cm) and poor recovery (22 cm) compared to the normal reference (<10 cm), with reproduction of the patient's symptoms during testing. Findings are consistent with convergence insufficiency. For doctor/orthoptist's review and consideration of vision therapy.

immediate: Confirm patient identity and explain the test: a target will be brought slowly towards her nose and she should try to keep it single for as long as possible, telling the examiner when it becomes double or blurry
Ensure patient is wearing her current glasses (distance correction) for the test, as ordered
Hold an accommodative target (e.g. small print on a stick, or a penlight with an accommodative target attached) at arm's length along the patient's midline at eye level
Slowly move the target towards the patient's eyes (nose) at a steady pace, asking her to report when the target becomes double (break point) or when one eye visibly drifts outward
Measure and record the distance from the bridge of the nose to the target at the break point
Slowly move the target away again and record the distance at which the patient reports the target becomes single again (recovery point)
Repeat the measurement at least 3 times to ensure consistency and document the range
Document the break and recovery points clearly, noting whether the patient's symptoms (eye strain, diplopia) were reproduced during testing
Hand findings to doctor/orthoptist along with the patient's symptom history
follow_up: Doctor/orthoptist to confirm diagnosis of convergence insufficiency and discuss management options, which may include convergence/vision therapy exercises (e.g. pencil push-ups)
Reassess NPC after a course of vision therapy to monitor improvement
Advise on review of study habits and breaks during prolonged near work
patient_education: Explain that convergence insufficiency means her eyes have difficulty turning inward together to focus on near objects for prolonged periods, which explains her symptoms while studying
Reassure her that this is a common and treatable condition, often improved with specific eye exercises
Advise her to take regular breaks during study sessions (e.g. the 20-20-20 rule) while awaiting further assessment

key_points: Confirms patient identity and elicits the pattern of symptoms: near-work-related eye strain, headaches, and intermittent diplopia relieved by looking away
Confirms patient is wearing her usual distance correction for the test as appropriate
Asks about the duration and intensity of near work (study habits, screen time)
Explains the NPC test procedure clearly before starting
Uses an appropriate accommodative target and brings it towards the patient's nose along the midline at a steady pace
Correctly identifies and measures the break point (where fixation is lost/diplopia reported) and recovery point
Repeats the measurement at least 3 times to ensure consistency and documents the range
Notes whether the patient's symptoms were reproduced during testing
Compares the measured break point (16 cm) against the normal reference (<10 cm) to identify it as receded
Recognises the pattern (receded break point, poor recovery, reproduced symptoms) as consistent with convergence insufficiency
Understands that convergence insufficiency commonly presents with near-work-related asthenopia in young adults
Does not prescribe vision therapy independently — refers to doctor/orthoptist for management plan
Documents break and recovery point measurements clearly and accurately
Hands findings to doctor/orthoptist along with relevant symptom history
Educates patient on the nature of convergence insufficiency and reassures that it is treatable
Advises on practical interim measures (breaks during near work) while awaiting further management
